vignette: Elias sits across from me, boots still damp from the morning tide, his knuckles mapped with old salt-lines and fresh cuts. At twenty-six, he carries his body like a vessel that has taken on water. When we speak, he does not look directly at me. His eyes track the condensation on his coffee cup, the seam of the floorboards, the distant horizon through the clinic window. He speaks in measured fragments, but the spaces between his words are heavy, filled with things he has not yet found the language to name. He tells me about the room. Concrete walls that sweat in the summer heat. The metal chair bolted to the floor. The systematic questions that never stop, just changing shape. The boots on his chest. The electric prods that turn his nerves into live wires. He does not describe the torture as a single moment but as a long, suffocating stretch of time where daylight becomes irrelevant and his own breath sounds like a foreign thing. They want names, coordinates, loyalties. He gives them silence. They keep going. When they finally let him walk out into the indifferent dawn, his body feels like borrowed equipment, too heavy to move, too light to trust. The return to the coast is not a homecoming but a recalibration. The first time he steps onto the quay, the smell of diesel and rotting kelp sends him doubling over, hands gripping the iron railing until his shoulders lock. He tells his wife, Mara, that the air feels thick, like breathing through wool. She brings him tea, sits beside him on the narrow bunk, and does not press. They have been married three years, but lately, he keeps a careful distance between them in bed, his body rigid, listening for the shift of floorboards that sounds like a boot heel. He loves her, but his nervous system has learned to mistake closeness for threat. He flinches when she reaches over to touch his shoulder. He wakes in the dark, calculating exits, wondering how long it would take him to run if the walls suddenly locked. He still fishes. The work demands it. Each morning, he climbs the gangway of his trawler, the same route he took for a decade before the room. He throws nets, checks engines, reads the water. But the sea has changed for him. The low rumble of the diesel engine matches the frequency of the generators that powered the interrogation lights. The sudden jerk of a winch sends his pulse to his throat. He catches himself scanning the horizon not for fish but for approaching boats, for threats, for escape routes. He tells me he used to love the rhythm of the work-the predictable pull of the tide, the camaraderie of the crew. Now, he works alone in his own head. When a deckhand drops a crate too hard, Elias crosses the deck in two strides, palms flat against the man's chest, breath short. He apologizes immediately, but the damage lingers. The ocean, once a sanctuary, sits heavy against his ribs like that concrete floor. He sleeps on the couch half the week. When he lies in bed, he wakes at the exact hour the guards change shifts in his memory, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape a chest that no longer contains him. He drinks less now, not out of wisdom but because the taste of grain alcohol reminds him of the water they force down his throat. He goes to the market, mends lines, kisses Mara's forehead before dawn. He is careful. He is watching. He is tired in a way that sleep does not touch. He sits with me still, offering pieces of himself in the quiet hours, waiting to see if the room will hold.
